I am 54 this year, farming 8 mu of land in Quzhou County. I finished middle school, so I can read the instructions on fertilizer bags and understand most of what the county extension agent says, but honestly, after 35 years on this land, I trust my own eyes and what the neighbors do more than any textbook. It is already spring, so my winter wheat is in the ground—I sowed it last October after rotary tilling the field, using improved varieties like Jimai 22 that I bought from the county seed station. I never save my own wheat seed; the yield drops too much. As for summer, I will plant Denghai 605 hybrid maize right after wheat harvest in early June. Everyone in my village does this wheat-maize double cropping. Cotton might pay more in a good year, but at my age my back is not what it used to be, and with my children working in Handan we do not have the hands for picking. 

For fertilizer, last year I used about 50 kg of compound fertilizer per mu at sowing for wheat, and topdressed with urea twice in spring—once at green-up and again at jointing. The technician tells us we use too much nitrogen, but I would rather spend a bit more on fertilizer than risk losing half the crop to poor soil. This land used to be alkaline and weak, so I will put down roughly 25 kg of nitrogen per mu for wheat and about 20 kg per mu for maize. I get my phosphorus and potassium from the compound bags—maybe 8 kg of each per mu for wheat, and 6 kg each for maize. Irrigation costs keep rising because of the electricity for the tube well, but I will still water the wheat four times total and the maize twice if the summer rains are scarce. For pesticides, I spray about four times on wheat and three times on maize, mainly herbicide, fungicide for rust, and insecticide if the corn borer shows up. I expect about 500 kg per mu from the wheat and around 550 kg per mu from the maize if the weather holds. That is enough to feed my family and leave some grain to sell.
